critical.title: SQL injection in the exported NotesProvider
critical.description: delete() concatenates the URI's last path segment straight into the SQL selection clause, and query() does the same through SQLiteQueryBuilder.appendWhere() at line 117. The provider is exported with no permission, so the URI -- and therefore the injected SQL -- comes from whichever app makes the call.
critical.impact: Any app installed on the device can read, alter or delete every row of divanotes.db by crafting a content:// URI. Because appendWhere() splices the value into the WHERE clause before the query is compiled, the injection also reaches rows the URI never addressed.
critical.code_snippet: count = this.mDB.delete(TABLE, "_id = " + id + (!TextUtils.isEmpty(selection) ? " AND (" + selection + ')' : ""), selectionArgs);

lines: count = this.mDB.delete(TABLE, "_id = " + id + (!TextUtils.isEmpty(selection) ? " AND (" + selection + ')' : ""), selectionArgs);

critical.exploitation: adb shell content query --uri "content://jakhar.aseem.diva.provider.notesprovider/notes/1 or 1=1--" returns every note rather than note 1. The same URI passed to ContentResolver.delete() from an unprivileged app empties the table.
critical.recommendation: Pass the path segment as a bound parameter -- selection "_id = ?" with selectionArgs {id} -- rather than concatenating it, and drop appendWhere() in favour of a parameterised selection. Then set android:exported="false" on the provider, or guard it with a signature-level permission if another app genuinely needs it.

components: Exported ContentProvider reachable by any installed app
SQL injection in the exported NotesProvider
flow: A malicious app resolves content://jakhar.aseem.diva.provider.notesprovider/notes -- no permission is required because the provider is exported.
It appends "1 or 1=1--" as the id path segment, which delete() and query() splice into the WHERE clause unparameterised.
SQLite evaluates the attacker's predicate, so every row of divanotes.db is returned or removed regardless of the id requested.

high.title: Application ships with android:debuggable="true"
high.description: The application element sets android:debuggable="true", so the shipped APK is debuggable on any device -- not only on a development build, and not only on a rooted one.
high.impact: Anyone with adb access can attach a debugger, run code inside the app's process as the app's own UID, and read its private data directory. Every storage-related finding below becomes trivially reachable.
high.exploitation: adb shell run-as jakhar.aseem.diva cat /data/data/jakhar.aseem.diva/shared_prefs/jakhar.aseem.diva_preferences.xml prints the saved credentials, with no root required, because the app is debuggable.
high.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable from the manifest. The Android Gradle plugin sets it per build type, so a release build gets false automatically and shipping it as true is almost always accidental.

high.title: Exported ContentProvider reachable by any installed app
high.description: NotesProvider is declared android:exported="true" with no android:permission, android:readPermission or android:writePermission, and no path-permission element. Any app on the device can call query(), insert(), update() and delete() on it.
high.impact: The notes database is world-accessible to other apps. On its own that exposes the stored notes; combined with the unparameterised SQL in the same class it hands an unprivileged app arbitrary SQL execution against that database.
high.exploitation: An app with no permissions at all calls getContentResolver().query(Uri.parse("content://jakhar.aseem.diva.provider.notesprovider/notes"), null, null, null, null) and reads every row.
high.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" unless another app must reach the provider. If it must, declare a signature-level permission and apply it with android:permission so only your own signed apps qualify.

medium.title: targetSdkVersion 23 trusts user-installed CA certificates
medium.description: Below targetSdkVersion 24 the platform's default trust anchors include the user certificate store, and no network security config overrides that here. Certificates installed by the device owner -- or by anyone who can get one installed -- are accepted for TLS.
medium.impact: An interception proxy whose CA the user has been persuaded to install can read and rewrite the app's HTTPS traffic without any warning in the app.
medium.exploitation: Install a proxy CA in the user certificate store, route the device through the proxy, and the app's TLS sessions are readable in cleartext -- which is how the app is normally instrumented during testing.
medium.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 24 or above, and declare a network security config that pins trust to the system store: <trust-anchors><certificates src="system"/></trust-anchors>.

medium.title: SQL injection in InsecureDataStorage2Activity.saveCredentials()
medium.description: Both form fields are concatenated into an INSERT statement passed to execSQL(), which accepts multiple statements separated by semicolons. Neither value is escaped or bound.
medium.impact: A value containing a quote corrupts the statement; one containing a quote and a semicolon executes attacker-chosen SQL against the ids2 database, including DROP TABLE.
medium.code_snippet: this.mDB.execSQL("INSERT INTO myuser VALUES ('" + usr.getText().toString() + "', '" + pwd.getText().toString() + "');");

lines: this.mDB.execSQL("INSERT INTO myuser VALUES ('" + usr.getText().toString() + "', '" + pwd.getText().toString() + "');");
Log.d("Diva", "Error occurred while inserting into database: " + e.getMessage());

medium.exploitation: Saving the username '); DROP TABLE myuser;-- closes the INSERT and executes the second statement, destroying the credential table.
medium.recommendation: Replace execSQL with ContentValues and SQLiteDatabase.insert(), which binds every value, or bind explicitly with execSQL(sql, bindArgs).

medium.title: SQL injection in SQLInjectionActivity.search()
medium.description: The search field's text is concatenated into a rawQuery() string between single quotes, with no escaping and no bound parameters. The sqliuser table it queries holds usernames, passwords and credit card numbers seeded at lines 23-25.
medium.impact: Anyone who can type into the search box reads the whole credentials table rather than the one row they searched for, because the predicate they supply replaces the intended one.
medium.code_snippet: Cursor cr = this.mDB.rawQuery("SELECT * FROM sqliuser WHERE user = '" + srchtxt.getText().toString() + "'", null);

lines: Cursor cr = this.mDB.rawQuery("SELECT * FROM sqliuser WHERE user = '" + srchtxt.getText().toString() + "'", null);

medium.exploitation: Entering ' or '1'='1 in the search field makes the WHERE clause always true, and the activity prints every user, password and credit card number it returns.
medium.recommendation: Use rawQuery("SELECT * FROM sqliuser WHERE user = ?", new String[]{srchtxt.getText().toString()}) so the value is bound rather than concatenated.

medium.title: Credentials written to external storage
medium.description: The username and password are written as user:password to .uinfo.txt at the root of external storage. On the API levels this app targets, external storage has no per-app access control, and the leading dot hides the file from a file browser without restricting anyone.
medium.impact: Every app holding READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE -- a permission users grant routinely -- can read the credentials, as can anyone who mounts the device or reads a backup.
medium.exploitation: adb shell cat /sdcard/.uinfo.txt prints the stored credentials; another installed app reads the same path with only READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE.
medium.recommendation: Never write credentials to shared storage. Keep them in the app's private directory encrypted under a KeyStore key, and scope any genuinely shared file to the minimum data required.

medium.title: Exported APICreds2Activity's PIN check is bypassed by an intent extra
medium.description: The activity is implicitly exported by the intent-filter declared at AndroidManifest.xml:19-23, and the PIN prompt it shows is decided entirely by the boolean intent extra read here. The extra defaults to true, but the caller supplies it, and when it is false the credentials are printed and the method returns before the prompt is ever shown.
medium.impact: The PIN gate is decoration: a caller that passes the extra as false skips it and the activity prints the TVEETER API key and password immediately.

lines: apicview.setText("TVEETER API Key: secrettveeterapikey\nAPI User name: diva2\nAPI Password: p@ssword2");
apicview.setText("Register yourself at http://payatu.com to get your PIN and then login with that PIN!");

medium.exploitation: adb shell am start -a jakhar.aseem.diva.action.VIEW_CREDS2 --ez check_pin false displays the credentials without a PIN.
medium.recommendation: Never let a caller-supplied extra decide an authorisation outcome. Keep the check server-side or behind a KeyStore-backed credential, and set android:exported="false".

medium.title: Exported APICredsActivity discloses API credentials to any app
medium.description: APICredsActivity declares an intent-filter and no android:exported attribute, so on targetSdkVersion 23 it is implicitly exported. Its only job is to display the API key, username and password hardcoded at APICredsActivity.java:14.
medium.impact: Any installed app can launch the activity with the jakhar.aseem.diva.action.VIEW_CREDS action and put the vendor API credentials on screen, outside whatever access control the app believes it has.
medium.exploitation: adb shell am start -a jakhar.aseem.diva.action.VIEW_CREDS opens the credential screen directly, without going through the app's menu.
medium.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" on activities that carry no cross-app contract. If an intent-filter is genuinely needed, move the secret out of the activity and require a signature-level permission.

medium.title: WebView loads a user-supplied URI with JavaScript enabled
medium.description: setJavaScriptEnabled(true) is applied to the WebView in onCreate, and get() then passes the text of an input field straight to loadUrl() with no scheme allow-list. file:// URIs are therefore loaded and scripted inside the app's own origin.
medium.impact: The WebView will render any local file the app can read -- including its own databases and shared_prefs -- and JavaScript running in that file:// origin can read them and exfiltrate the contents.
medium.exploitation: Entering file:///data/data/jakhar.aseem.diva/shared_prefs/jakhar.aseem.diva_preferences.xml renders the stored credentials inside the app's own WebView.
medium.recommendation: Allow only https and reject every other scheme before calling loadUrl(). Disable JavaScript unless the content requires it, and set setAllowFileAccess(false) so local files cannot be reached at all.

medium.title: API key and password hardcoded in APICreds2Activity
medium.description: The TVEETER API key secrettveeterapikey and the account diva2 / p@ssword2 are string literals in the branch that runs once the PIN check is skipped.
medium.impact: A second set of vendor credentials ships inside the APK and is readable without running the app. The PIN prompt in front of them does not protect the literals themselves.
medium.code_snippet: apicview.setText("TVEETER API Key: secrettveeterapikey\nAPI User name: diva2\nAPI Password: p@ssword2");

lines: apicview.setText("TVEETER API Key: secrettveeterapikey\nAPI User name: diva2\nAPI Password: p@ssword2");
apicview.setText("Register yourself at http://payatu.com to get your PIN and then login with that PIN!");

medium.exploitation: Decompiling the APK shows the literal in onCreate; no PIN and no device access are needed to read it.
medium.recommendation: Remove the literals and fetch credentials at runtime over an authenticated channel, storing anything long-lived in the Android KeyStore.

medium.title: API key and password hardcoded in APICredsActivity
medium.description: The API key 123secretapikey123 and the account diva / p@ssword are string literals compiled into the activity, so they live in classes.dex in every copy of the app.
medium.impact: The credentials are recoverable from the APK alone -- no device, no running app, no user. Every install shares them, so rotating them means shipping a new build.
medium.code_snippet: apicview.setText("API Key: 123secretapikey123\nAPI User name: diva\nAPI Password: p@ssword");

lines: apicview.setText("API Key: 123secretapikey123\nAPI User name: diva\nAPI Password: p@ssword");

medium.exploitation: strings classes.dex | grep -i apikey, or any decompiler, prints the key straight out of the shipped APK.
medium.recommendation: Move the credential server-side and have the app obtain a short-lived token. If a secret must sit on the device, store it in the Android KeyStore, which keeps key material out of the app's own readable storage.

medium.title: Credentials written to SharedPreferences in cleartext
medium.description: The username and password are written to the default SharedPreferences with putString() and committed. SharedPreferences is an XML file in the app's data directory with no encryption of any kind.
medium.impact: The credentials sit in plaintext at /data/data/jakhar.aseem.diva/shared_prefs/jakhar.aseem.diva_preferences.xml, readable through adb run-as on this debuggable build, by any process running as the app's UID, and by anything that can read a backup.
medium.exploitation: adb shell run-as jakhar.aseem.diva cat shared_prefs/jakhar.aseem.diva_preferences.xml prints both values.
medium.recommendation: Do not persist raw credentials. Where a secret must be stored, encrypt it with a key held in the Android KeyStore -- EncryptedSharedPreferences does exactly this and is a drop-in replacement for this call.

medium.title: Credentials written to a readable temporary file
medium.description: A temporary file is created in the app's data directory, explicitly marked readable and writable with setReadable(true) and setWritable(true), and the username and password are written to it as user:password. The file is never deleted.
medium.impact: The credentials persist in a file whose permissions were deliberately widened, so anything running as the app's UID -- or anyone with adb on this debuggable build -- can read them long after the screen is closed.
medium.exploitation: adb shell run-as jakhar.aseem.diva ls /data/data/jakhar.aseem.diva | grep uinfo then cat the file; it holds the credentials in cleartext.
medium.recommendation: Drop the setReadable/setWritable calls -- the default private mode is already correct -- delete the file when finished, and keep credentials out of files entirely in favour of KeyStore-backed storage.

medium.title: Credit card number written to the system log
medium.description: The exception handler logs the full contents of the credit card field with Log.e under the tag diva-log. processCC() throws unconditionally at line 30, so this path runs on every checkout attempt rather than only in an unexpected error.
medium.impact: Cardholder data reaches logcat on every use. Log output is collected by crash reporters and device log tools, and on a debuggable build it is readable over adb.
medium.code_snippet: Log.e("diva-log", "Error while processing transaction with credit card: " + cctxt.getText().toString());

lines: Log.e("diva-log", "Error while processing transaction with credit card: " + cctxt.getText().toString());
Toast.makeText(this, "An error occured. Please try again later", 0).show();

medium.exploitation: adb logcat -s diva-log while using the checkout screen prints each card number entered.
medium.recommendation: Never log cardholder data. Log an error code or a masked value, strip the value from the exception path, and keep verbose logging out of release builds.

medium.title: Vendor access key hardcoded in HardcodeActivity
medium.description: The access check compares user input against the string literal vendorsecretkey with String.equals(). The secret it is meant to protect is in the comparison itself.
medium.impact: The gate can be passed by anyone who reads the APK, and the same key is valid in every installation, so revoking it requires a new release.

lines: Toast.makeText(this, "Access granted! See you on the other side :)", 0).show();
Toast.makeText(this, "Access denied! See you in hell :D", 0).show();

medium.exploitation: apktool d DIVA.apk then grep -r vendorsecretkey recovers the key; typing it into the field grants access.
medium.recommendation: Verify secrets server-side, or compare against a value derived from a KeyStore-backed key. A literal in the comparison is equivalent to publishing it.

low.title: Exception details written to the debug log
low.description: The failed-insert handler logs the exception message with Log.d. A SQLite exception message quotes the statement that failed, and the statement built one line earlier embeds both form fields, so the log line carries the credentials. The same pattern repeats at InsecureDataStorage2Activity.java:22, SQLInjectionActivity.java:27 and :47, InsecureDataStorage3Activity.java:34 and InsecureDataStorage4Activity.java:35.
low.impact: Failed writes leak the query -- and the credentials inside it -- into logcat. This is the low-severity tail of the same problem as the credit card logging above.
low.code_snippet: Log.d("Diva", "Error occurred while inserting into database: " + e.getMessage());

lines: this.mDB.execSQL("INSERT INTO myuser VALUES ('" + usr.getText().toString() + "', '" + pwd.getText().toString() + "');");
Log.d("Diva", "Error occurred while inserting into database: " + e.getMessage());

low.exploitation: adb logcat -s Diva while saving credentials that break the SQL prints the statement, including the values entered.
low.recommendation: Log an identifier rather than the exception text, and strip debug logging from release builds with a ProGuard rule or a logging wrapper that compiles out below a level.

low.title: Notes database is created unencrypted and pre-seeded with personal notes
low.description: DBHelper passes the database name straight to the stock SQLiteOpenHelper constructor -- no passphrase, no cipher -- and onCreate() then seeds six personal notes as string literals. The same database is what the exported provider serves.
low.impact: Note contents are stored in a plain SQLite file in the app's data directory and are readable by anything that can reach that directory -- which, on this debuggable build with an exported provider, is a low bar.

lines: private static class DBHelper extends SQLiteOpenHelper {
db.execSQL("INSERT INTO notes(title,note) VALUES ('office', '10 Meetings. 5 Calls. Lunch with CEO');");
db.execSQL("INSERT INTO notes(title,note) VALUES ('home', 'Buy toys for baby, Order dinner');");
db.execSQL("INSERT INTO notes(title,note) VALUES ('holiday', 'Either Goa or Amsterdam');");
db.execSQL("INSERT INTO notes(title,note) VALUES ('Expense', 'Spent too much on home theater');");
db.execSQL("INSERT INTO notes(title,note) VALUES ('Exercise', 'Alternate days running');");
public void onUpgrade(SQLiteDatabase db, int oldVersion, int newVersion) {

low.exploitation: adb shell run-as jakhar.aseem.diva sqlite3 databases/divanotes.db 'select * from notes;' dumps every note without touching the app.
low.recommendation: Encrypt the database at rest -- SQLCipher, or a KeyStore-derived key -- and seed sample content from a fixture rather than compiling it into the class.

info.title: Application data is backup-enabled
info.description: android:allowBackup="true" is set explicitly, so the app's private data directory is included in adb backup and in cloud backups, with no android:fullBackupContent rule excluding anything.
info.impact: Everything the storage findings above write -- SharedPreferences, the temp file, the notes database -- leaves the device inside a backup archive that is easier to reach than the device's own storage.
info.exploitation: adb backup -f diva.ab jakhar.aseem.diva produces an archive containing the app's private files.
info.recommendation: Set android:allowBackup="false", or declare android:fullBackupContent with an exclude rule for anything holding credentials.

info.title: Cleartext HTTP traffic is permitted by default
info.description: usesCleartextTraffic defaults to true below targetSdkVersion 28, and nothing here overrides it. The app holds the INTERNET permission, so plain HTTP requests are allowed.
info.impact: Any HTTP request the app makes is readable and modifiable on the network path. No such request was found in the decompiled code, which is why this is reported as information rather than as a network finding.
info.exploitation: Not directly exploitable as shipped -- no cleartext endpoint was located in the code.
info.recommendation: Set android:usesCleartextTraffic="false", or express the same in a network security config, so a future HTTP call fails loudly rather than silently sending in the clear.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The application element declares no android:networkSecurityConfig, so TLS trust and cleartext policy are left entirely to the platform defaults for targetSdkVersion 23.
info.impact: This is the reason the two network findings above stand: with no config, user CAs are trusted and cleartext is permitted, and there is no per-domain pinning or exception list.
info.exploitation: Not directly exploitable. It is the missing control behind the two network findings.
info.recommendation: Add a network security config that trusts only the system store, disables cleartext, and pins the domains the app actually talks to.

info.title: Two dangerous permissions requested
info.description: The manifest requests WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE and READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, both in the dangerous protection level, alongside the normal-level INTERNET. External storage is used by InsecureDataStorage4Activity to write credentials.
info.impact: Dangerous permissions widen what a compromise of the app reaches. Reported for context: they are declared, and one of them is used to store credentials off the app's private directory.
info.exploitation: Not directly exploitable. It is the capability the external-storage finding above depends on.
info.recommendation: Drop both if the credential file moves into private storage, which is the fix recommended for that finding.

info.title: minSdkVersion 15 admits devices without modern platform defences
info.description: The app installs on Android 4.0.3 and later. Those releases lack scoped storage, runtime permissions, the modern network security config and current WebView hardening.
info.impact: On the oldest supported devices several of the findings above have no platform-level mitigation at all, and the WebView is serviced by the system image rather than updated independently.
info.exploitation: Not directly exploitable. It sets the floor for how much the platform helps.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to a currently supported level; each step removes a class of these fallbacks.

refuted.title: Hardcoded encryption key in DivaJni
refuted.description: A pattern match on the string literal soName in a class that loads a native library was reported as a hardcoded encryption key.
refuted.impact: None. The cited lines declare a library name and two native method signatures.
refuted.recommendation: No change required. The native library itself is out of scope for source analysis and is covered separately by the binary checks.

reasons: The cited lines contain none of AES, SecretKeySpec, Cipher, javax.crypto or KeyGenerator -- nothing in them constructs or holds a key.
The matched literal "divajni" is the argument to System.loadLibrary, which is a library name, not key material.
